answer: The 'continue + label' feature in Java allows the program to skip the rest of the current iteration and move to the labeled loop [3]. query: What is the difference between virtual functions and pure virtual functions?
answer: The difference between virtual functions and pure virtual functions is that virtual functions have a definition in the base class, whereas pure virtual functions have no definition in the base class and must be implemented by any derived classes [1][2]. Virtual functions can be overridden by derived classes, but they do not have to be, whereas pure virtual functions must be implemented by derived classes or they will also become abstract classes [2].

query: What is the purpose of a virtual destructor in C++?
answer: The purpose of a virtual destructor in C++ is to ensure that when a derived object is deleted through a base class pointer, the destructors of both the derived class and the base class are invoked [1][2][3]. This is necessary to prevent memory leaks and ensure proper cleanup of resources. If a destructor is not declared as virtual in the base class, only the base class's destructor will be invoked when the object is deleted, potentially leading to memory leaks [1][3]. By declaring the destructor as virtual, the correct destructor for the actual object being deleted will be called, regardless of the type of pointer used to delete it [1][3].

Language FMs: Transformer-based models (BERT, GPT-style) that treat biological sequences (DNA, RNA, protein) like text — reading them as strings of "tokens" the same way a sentence is made of words. Vision FMs: Originally built for image tasks (CNNs like AlexNet/ResNet). In bioinformatics, these get repurposed for biological data that has spatial or grid-like structure — e.g. VQ-VAE models that tokenize DNA almost like breaking an image into patches.

Large Language Models in Bioinformatics: A Survey (2025)

Zhenyu Wang, Zikang Wang, Jiyue Jiang, Pengan Chen, Xiangyu Shi, Yu Li

(https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.184/)

General Idea

Bioinformatics deals with analyzing complex biological data — DNA, RNA, proteins, single-cell data — using computational methods

This paper surveys how Large Language Models (LLMs), the same class of models behind ChatGPT, are now being applied to these biological problems

Biological sequences (like DNA: ATCGGTA...) can be treated like "language" and fed into transformer-based models the same way text is

The paper maps out what's been built, what works, and what remains unsolved

Model Architectures in Bioinformatics

Encoder-only (e.g. BERT-style): Reads the entire sequence bidirectionally (looks left AND right at every token)

Main job: read input, learn rich internal representation i.e. create embeddings (vector representations)

Because it looks left & right, retains a lot of context/captures dependencies well -> in biology, “tokens” in the sequence can depend heavily on neighbours and even on tokens super far away

Great for classification and prediction tasks (e.g. "does this DNA sequence bind to this protein?")

Cannot generate new sequences

Decoder-only (e.g. GPT-style): Generates sequences token by token, only looking at previous tokens (unidirectional)

Autoregressive decoding, just like the LLMs we use

Good for generating novel DNA/protein sequences

Weaker at tasks requiring full-sequence understanding cause it never looks forward (when predicting, you never look at the next token you’re going to predict, only all the tokens leading up to this one)

Any generator is always going to be limited by its parameters–requires fine-tuning for domain-specific problems

Encoder-Decoder (e.g. T5/RoseTTAFold): Combines both — encodes input into a rich representation, then decodes into structured output

Best for sequence-to-sequence tasks (e.g. "given this RNA sequence, predict its 3D structure")

Most computationally expensive (~81GB VRAM, ~40 days to train on average)

Main Subdomains Covered

1. DNA & Genomics — Models learn from DNA sequences to predict things like which regions regulate gene expression, where proteins bind to DNA, and what effect mutations have on disease.

ol and PMDM (generate 3D molecules designed to fit a specific protein's binding pocket — useful for targeted drug design)

DrugBAN (predicts drug-target interactions using attention mechanisms to highlight which parts of the drug and target matter most). Single-Cell Analysis

Single-cell sequencing measures gene activity in individual cells rather than averaging across millions of cells, revealing cell-level biological differences. Key tasks:

Cell clustering: Grouping similar cells together based on gene expression patterns, without knowing in advance what type each cell is (an unsupervised task — no labels given upfront). Cell type annotation: Once cells are grouped, labeling what kind of cell each group actually is (e.g. "this cluster is T-cells"). Multi-omics integration: Combining multiple types of data measured from the same cells — e.g. gene expression plus chromatin accessibility (which parts of the DNA are "open" and available to be read/used) — into one unified analysis. Notable models:

scGPT (general-purpose pre-training + fine-tuning for clustering, batch correction, and gene network inference)

scBERT (cell type annotation, designed to reduce "batch effects" — technical variation between different experimental batches that isn't real biological signal)

scFoundation (100M parameters, handles ~20,000 genes simultaneously)

GLUE (integrates multiple omics types together and infers regulatory relationships between them — an example of a graph-based multimodal FM)

DeepMAPS and MarsGT (use graph transformers to build cell-gene relationship networks, useful for finding rare cell populations). Data Resources (useful for picking a FYP dataset)

Public databases listed by domain:

Genomics: TCGA (cancer genomic data, 2.5 petabytes), ENCODE

Transcriptomics: GEO (7.3 billion data points)

Proteomics: UniProt, PDB (Protein Data Bank — 3D structures)

Drug discovery: ChEMBL, ZINC, PubChem

Single-cell: Human Cell Atlas, Single-Cell Expression Atlas

Key Challenges / Future Directions

Pre-training paradigm gaps: Techniques like prompt learning (giving the model task hints during fine-tuning) and contrastive learning (training by comparing similar vs. dissimilar examples) are still underexplored for biological data specifically. Evaluation gaps: No standardized way to fairly benchmark different foundation models against each other across bioinformatics tasks yet.
